title: Department of Labor Resources Help Veterans Build Strong Careers
summary:
Across the country, Veterans are preparing for life after service. Many know that VA helps them transition, but fewer realize the Department of Labor has an entire agency focused on helping Veterans, transitioning service members, and military spouses find meaningful careers.

In this episode of At the Table, I sat down with Jeremiah Workman, Assistant Secretary of the Department of Labor’s Veterans Employment and Training Service. 

We talked about how DOL programs support Veterans, why skilled trades and defense related careers are such strong fits, and how Veterans can explore opportunities in trucking, manufacturing, and the defense industrial base.

Assistant Secretary Workman explains how programs like the Transition Assistance Program, Jobs for Veterans State Grants, and USERRA protections meet Veterans wherever they are in their journey. 

He also highlights why careers in welding, electrical work, trucking, and other trades provide long term stability and purpose.

Veterans who want to explore trade careers or apprenticeships can visit their nearest American Job Center or browse thousands of opportunities at https:/apprenticeship.gov.

title: How Flock Cameras Cut Beverly Hills Crime 34%
summary:
Retired Beverly Hills Police Chief Mark Stainbrook sits down with Your LEO Nation and walks through the system he built after his first night on the job — the night Jacqueline Avant was murdered.

He covers the constitutional fight over Flock cameras and ALPRs, why public streets are not a privacy zone, and how BHPD combined license-plate readers at every entrance, live cameras, and drones into a military-style command center. Stolen-car recoveries jumped from about 50 a year to more than 200. Arrests rose 22%. Career criminals got a “jail card” warning them: come here to steal, and this technology will find you.

Stainbrook also tells the story of a suspect tied to four murders in four days whose plate hit coming into the city — officers were on the car in two minutes, recovered the gun, and ballistics linked the killings. He breaks down audits, two-year video retention, supervisor oversight, fewer bad stops, lower liability, and why 600-plus agencies came to study the model.

America has lost a friend and a patriot, and so have I. Sam Faddis—retired CIA operations officer, frequent guest on this show, and a man who became my friend even though I never met him in person—passed away quietly at the University of Pennsylvania in Philadelphia on the evening of July 25, 2026 with his wife, four children, and family by his side. I read the statement from his family, who asked for privacy and thanked the doctors, medical staff, and all of you for your prayers and support. I first came across Sam through Hillsdale College’s free Imprimis, where he wrote about what had gone wrong at the CIA and how to fix it—brave, objective, and always productive. Sam told the truth about everything, including how to right this ship. We’ll miss him terribly.

title: The 2011 Realignment of Adult Felony Populations: Results and Key Takeaways
summary: In 2011, California shifted responsibility for incarcerating and supervising certain adult felony populations from the state to counties. The state also shifted a portion of tax revenues to counties to cover the additional costs. These changes were part of a larger shift of responsibilities known as the 2011 realignment. Pursuant to Chapter 96 of 2023 (AB 1080, Ta), this report provides information on how various aspects of the realignment of adult felony populations have been implemented and evaluates the results.
